grant_challenge.constraint: Propose one small, testable intervention. No major construction or police crackdown. Explain who maintains it.
grant_challenge.display_note: Show this card’s budget and pilot scope with the 30-day challenge beside question 6.
grant_challenge.budget_policy: Each card has a proposed classroom pilot budget in BDT, scaled to the pilot scope. These are discussion constraints, not verified procurement estimates.

cards.title: TRAFFIC JAM
cards.focus: A crowded Saheb Bazar street where people and goods compete for limited road space.
tiles: Pedestrians squeeze through a narrow opening between slow vehicles.
A walker steps into traffic because goods fill the footpath.
A driver stops in the moving lane to let a passenger out.
A worker loads boxes from a handcart while vehicles wait behind.
Two vehicles compete for a curb with no clear place to pick up riders.
A shop worker rushes boxes from a vehicle to a doorway during a busy period.
questions: Which two scenes would slow a person on foot most?
When has a crowded Rajshahi street delayed you? What happened?
Should the curb serve passengers or shop deliveries first? Why?
Why might a driver stop in the lane even when it delays others?
If loading is banned at busy times, who might lose income?
What one street-space change would your grant test?

grant.pilot_scope: Pilot one safer pickup or delivery zone on a short Saheb Bazar segment.

cards.title: POWER CUT

When did a power cut last change your plans in Rajshahi?
Should a shared backup power point serve students or shops first? Why?
Why might a shop use a smoky generator despite the cost?
If one building offers free charging, what new problem might appear?
What one backup-power idea would your grant test?

grant.pilot_scope: Pilot backup light and charging for one shared study area.

evidence.basis: supplied brief plus Rajshahi student reporting

A rider steers around a barrier to reach the other side of the road.

cards.title: BROKEN FOOTPATHS

cards.title: GROUNDWATER DROP
cards.focus: Falling groundwater in the Barind area puts irrigation and household water needs under pressure.
tiles: A farmer lowers a rope farther into a well before reaching water.
A farmer presses dry cracked soil beside young crops.
A farmer keeps a pump running to water a field in the dry season.
A resident carries containers from a distant working water point.

Rainwater runs off a farm edge while a farmer looks at an empty storage basin.
questions: Which two scenes show water becoming harder to reach?

cards.title: PREPAID METER
cards.focus: A Rajshahi renter has a flat-specific NESCO prepaid meter in a caged downstairs bank, with no easy live remote balance check and a recharge token that must be keyed in at the meter.
tiles: A renter walks downstairs from a flat toward a bank of separate electric meters.
A renter opens the protective cage door and presses a prepaid meter keypad through the open doorway.
A renter refreshes a meter account on a phone while remaining upstairs.
A renter makes a phone payment after the fan and lights have stopped.
A phone shows an older balance bar while the meter display shows a lower one.
A renter reads a long recharge PIN on a phone and keys it into a downstairs meter with the cage door fully open.
questions: Which two scenes make checking the balance inconvenient?
Have you had to go downstairs to check or recharge a meter?
Would a live phone balance or a low-balance alert help more? Why?
Why does an online payment still require a trip to this meter?
If an alert is sent daily, what new annoyance or error might follow?
What one balance-or-recharge pilot would your grant test?

grant.pilot_scope: Test a building-level way to read each flat’s balance remotely or deliver dependable low-balance alerts, without assuming NESCO offers a live API or remote token entry.

evidence.basis: user report plus NESCO guidance and keypad-recharge instructions
evidence.editor_note: The meter arrangement, delayed remote reading, need to enter a token after an online purchase, and unusually long PIN messages are the user’s reported experience. NESCO documents meter short codes; the payment provider says keypad meters require token entry. A 2026 Sylhet report documents 80–240-digit prepaid tokens in Bangladesh; it does not establish the frequency for NESCO customers in Rajshahi.
evidence.user_detail: The user reports that each flat usually has its own meter, the meter bank is often caged below the building, the website reading updates about once daily, and some recharge PIN messages reach about 100 characters.

cards.title: HARD WATER
cards.focus: In one rented Rajshahi building, reported high-TDS water with iron and calcium leaves stains and scale, damages taps, and drives repeated strong-cleaner use.
tiles: A thick white ring builds around a bathroom tap and slows the stream.
Orange-brown marks spread below a running bathroom faucet.
A renter scrubs mineral marks from bathroom tiles.
A plumber removes another worn tap while the renter holds a new fitting.
A cleaner wearing gloves applies a strong liquid to stained bathroom tiles.
A renter and landlord examine stained fixtures beside an unused sample bottle.
questions: Which two scenes show what the water leaves behind?
What water marks or maintenance problems have you seen in Rajshahi?
Should the first money go to water testing or sturdier taps? Why?
Why might renters keep buying strong cleaner instead of fixing the source?
If residents use more strong cleaner, what problem may follow?
What one water-and-fixture pilot would your grant test?

grant.pilot_scope: Test water in one building, document iron and hardness, and trial a practical fixture or treatment response.

evidence.basis: user report plus Rajshahi water research
evidence.editor_note: The renter reports the high TDS and iron/calcium; TDS alone does not measure hardness. A local sample would need testing.
evidence.user_detail: The renter uses Damp Fix for stubborn deposits; its exact formulation is not assumed here.

What one toilet-access change would your grant test?
